scenes.narration: Try to tickle yourself. Go on. Nothing, right?
scenes.art: a young adult trying to tickle their own ribs with a deadpan bored expression, nothing happening

scenes.narration: That's not a glitch. Your brain is doing it on purpose.
scenes.art: a cute cartoon brain character wearing a tiny referee whistle, holding up a stop hand, confident smile

scenes.narration: Every time you move, your brain predicts what that movement is going to feel like.
scenes.art: a cute cartoon brain looking into a glowing crystal ball that shows a hand about to touch an arm

scenes.narration: That prediction is used to turn the feeling down. It's why your own touch feels so flat.
scenes.art: a cute cartoon brain turning down a big glowing volume dial, a hand touching an arm in the background

scenes.narration: Scientists tested this with a tickle robot. You move a handle, and a robot strokes your palm.
scenes.art: a friendly cute robot arm stroking an open human palm with a soft foam pad, a person holding a handle on the other side

scenes.narration: With no delay, it barely tickles. But add a delay of up to a fifth of a second, and it gets more and more ticklish.
scenes.art: a cartoon stopwatch beside a palm being stroked by a robot, wavy tickle lines getting stronger, giggling face

scenes.narration: The delay breaks the prediction. Suddenly, the touch feels like it's coming from someone else.
scenes.art: a surprised young adult laughing as a mysterious friendly shadow hand tickles them

scenes.narration: Scientists think this helps you notice what isn't you. A spider on your arm matters more than your own sleeve.
scenes.art: a tiny cartoon spider walking on an arm with a glowing alert outline, while the sleeve fades into the background

scenes.narration: Here's the twist. In one study, some patients who hear voices rated their own touch as just as intense as someone else's.
scenes.art: a calm young adult sitting in a quiet research room touching their own palm, soft sound waves floating around their head, gentle and respectful mood

scenes.narration: Researchers think the brain's self-check may not be tagging their own actions as their own.
scenes.art: a cartoon brain with a name tag stamp machine, a few actions slipping past without a name tag

scenes.narration: So if you can't tickle yourself, good news. Your brain knows you're you.
scenes.art: a happy young adult giving a thumbs up while a smiling cartoon brain floats above them with a heart

scenes.narration: Now be honest. Did you just try?

post.title: Why you can't tickle yourself (your brain is doing it on purpose) 🧠
post.description:
Your brain predicts your own touch and turns it down. Scientists proved it with a tickle robot, and the exceptions are fascinating.

Sources:
Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (2000) NeuroReport
Blakemore et al. (1999) Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
Blakemore et al. (2000) Psychological Medicine
